why: The proposition states the legal basis on which the Methodology was developed, which concerns the text itself rather than markets or undertakings.

The proposition states what the Methodology covers: it sets the procedure for establishing dominance and applies to the activities of undertakings, groups and consumers on national and regional markets, with listed objects of analysis.

The proposition opens by stating the purposes and proceedings for which dominance is established (demonopolisation, antimonopoly regulation, control of concerted actions and concentrations, enforcement of competition law), which answers question 2 before the glossary of definitions that follows is reached.

This is the lead-in to the list of stages of the AMCU's analysis: it says that establishing a monopoly (dominant) position may include the actions that follow, so it describes how the analysis is done rather than being a bare heading.

This item belongs to the list of analysis stages and tells the AMCU what to establish as the objects of analysis: the undertaking or group of undertakings and the specific product it supplies or acquires, so it is not an empty stage heading.

This item is one stage in the list of stages for establishing dominance, and it tells the AMCU to compile a list of products that have the features of a single product or product group, which is a step it must take rather than a bare heading.

It is an item in the list of stages for establishing a monopoly (dominant) position, and it directs the AMCU to take a concrete analytical step: compile a list of the main sellers and buyers of the goods, so it is more than a heading.
It is a bare stage name ("Визначення товарних меж ринку.") that asserts nothing and only structures the text, which the hard-case rule types as housekeeping.
It is a bare stage name ("Defining the territorial (geographic) boundaries of the market.") that asserts nothing and only structures the text, which the hard-case rule types as housekeeping.

This item belongs to the 2002 list of stages for establishing dominance and tells the AMCU to establish the time period for which the undertakings' position is assessed, i.e. to define the market's temporal boundaries; it is a step of the analysis, not a bare heading.
This is a bare stage name ("Визначення обсягів товару, який обертається на ринку.") that asserts no criterion, method or step on its own, so under the hard-case rule it only structures the text.
It is a bare stage name ('Calculation of market shares of undertakings') that asserts nothing on its own and only structures the text, like the protocol's heading example.

This item in the list of analysis stages tells the AMCU to compile a list of sellers and buyers, including potential competitors able to sell or buy the same or analogous product, and specifies who belongs on it, so it goes beyond a bare stage name.

As item 10 of the ordered list of stages in point 2.1, it requires the AMCU to determine entry and exit barriers for actual and potential sellers and buyers of the same or analogous product, so it is a substantive analytical step rather than a bare heading.
The proposition is a bare stage name with no verb, criterion or consequence, so under the hard-case rule it only structures the text.

It allows the AMCU to change the number and order of the stages set out in point 2.1 according to the facts of the case, such as the product, the market structure and the information available, which is a rule about how the analysis is done.

It sets what the dominance analysis covers by listing its objects: an undertaking, a group of undertakings, and the specific product they produce, supply, sell or buy; it gives no criterion for how the analysis is done.

It sets out what the dominance analysis covers by adding public authorities, local self-government bodies and administrative-economic management and control bodies as objects of analysis, but only for their economic activity.
It sets out the method for determining which entities make up the undertaking: the AMCU lists all legal and natural persons linked by relations of control, a step it applies to the facts of a case.

It sets out how the AMCU determines the composition of a group of undertakings, by listing the independent undertakings that include the entity producing, supplying, selling or acquiring the specific product, which is a method the analysis applies to a case.

It sets the criterion for which goods go on the list for assessing dominance: goods circulating in Ukraine or the relevant part of its territory that sellers and buyers treat as the same (similar, analogous) product. That is a test the analysis applies to the facts, not a mere definition.

It states the criterion by which the AMCU identifies the features of a single (similar, analogous) product or product group, namely their similarity, which the analysis applies to the facts of a case.

It lists the consumer characteristics (functional purpose, physical, technical and operational characteristics, degree of novelty) that serve as criteria for compiling the list of goods for which a dominant position is assessed, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

This list item names the conditions of consumption (energy or water supply needs, specific placement or installation, level of technical servicing and transport) that the AMCU takes into account when grouping goods into the product list, so it is a factor a decision applies to the facts rather than a bare definition of a term.

It lists sale conditions (wholesale or direct contracts including barter and tolling schemes, retail including branded chains, additional services and benefits) that the AMCU takes into account when determining the list of goods and their sellers and buyers, so it is a criterion applied in the analysis.

The fragment 'Цін.' (prices) appears to be one item in a list of factors or sources the AMCU uses to determine the products and their main sellers and buyers, so it states a criterion the analysis applies rather than structuring the text; this rests on the inferred list context, since the item alone asserts nothing.

It gives the AMCU a criterion for compiling the list of goods at this stage: intermediate outputs consumed in the undertaking's own production and not sold on the market are left out of the goods analysed, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a method for compiling the list of main sellers and buyers and sets a threshold (as a rule above 5 percent of known volumes) for what counts as significant volumes, which the AMCU can apply to the facts of a case.

It states the method for defining the product boundaries of a market: forming a group of interchangeable goods using listed interchangeability indicators (similar purpose and properties, common consumers, no significant price difference, supply-side substitutability), with the option to split or merge groups, which a decision can apply to a case.

Despite the 'must take into account' framing, the proposition only says what interchangeable goods are (a homogeneous group the consumer treats as the same product, standardized or differentiated) and gives no method, threshold or step for drawing the product boundaries.

It says what counts as 'standardized goods' (goods sharing a common system of indicators and the same technical standards, specifications or application standards), and it only classifies without stating how the product boundaries of the market are drawn.

It says what differentiated goods (product groups) are, namely goods whose differences in properties, appearance, quality, service and the like let consumers tell them apart from similar goods, without stating how the product boundaries of a market are drawn.

It states the method for defining the geographic boundaries of a market (the minimum territory beyond which purchase is impossible or impractical for the consumer), lists the factors that may be taken into account, and gives a decisive rule (the lower mobility of demand or supply), all of which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a method the AMCU may use to verify the territorial boundaries of a market, namely examining the market's openness to interregional and/or international trade, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It sets out an indicator (degree of market openness), its calculation formula, and thresholds (30% for regional, 40% for national markets) that tell the AMCU how to read the result when setting the market's geographic boundaries, which a decision can apply directly to a case.
Beyond defining temporal market boundaries, it sets an applicable criterion: the period during which the market has a stable structure, by default one year, which a decision can apply to a case.

It states a criterion for setting the temporal boundaries of the market when the capital turnover period exceeds one year, namely one to three such periods, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It sets the conditions under which a period shorter than one year may be recognised as the temporal boundaries of the market and fixes a 5 percent threshold for a significant price increase, both criteria a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states the method for calculating market volume (a summation formula over undertakings' volumes within the market's product and temporal boundaries) and a rule for when physical versus value indicators are used, which a decision applies to the facts of a case.

It sets out the method and formula for calculating an undertaking's volume of goods sold or purchased within the product and temporal boundaries of the market, which is applied to compute market shares.

It sets out the formula and its components by which the AMCU calculates the volume of goods sold or purchased by each undertaking for computing market shares, a method a decision applies to the facts of a case.

It states the method (a formula: the undertaking's volume of sales or purchases divided by market volume, times 100) by which the AMCU calculates an undertaking's market share, which a decision applies to the facts of a case.
It sets out the formula by which the AMCU calculates the combined market share of the two to five largest undertakings, a method applied to the facts of a case.
It states a method the AMCU may use: when reliable volume data are lacking, market shares may be calculated from estimates, production capacities or other indicators of sales or purchase volumes.
It says which undertakings count as potential competitors by listing three categories, and says nothing about how the AMCU must use them in defining the market or establishing dominance.

It says what barriers to entry for potential competitors are by listing the kinds of restrictions that count, without stating how the AMCU assesses them or what follows for market definition or dominance.

It states a criterion with a time threshold (a barrier not overcome within 1–2 years because entry costs cannot be recovered) that the AMCU applies to conclude that an undertaking is not a potential competitor.
It introduces the list of actions that establishing a monopoly (dominant) position consists of, so it states the steps the AMCU must take rather than being a bare heading.

This item in the list of steps for establishing dominance tells the AMCU what to calculate, namely the undertaking's own share and the combined shares of the two to five largest undertakings, so it is an analytical step that goes beyond a bare stage name.

It states the market-share thresholds of Article 12 of the Law (35% for one undertaking, 50% for two or three, 70% for four or five) that the AMCU applies when establishing a dominant position, so it is a threshold the analysis applies even though it restates the statute.

As an item in the list of stages for establishing dominance, it tells the AMCU to rebut, where needed, the respondent's arguments that it holds no monopoly (dominant) position, which is a step of the analysis rather than a bare heading.

It states the market-share thresholds (over 35 percent for a single undertaking, and combined shares over 70 or 50 percent for the largest two to five undertakings) that the AMCU applies to recognise a monopoly (dominant) position, which is a threshold a decision can apply to a case.

It sets out the steps the AMCU must take to establish dominance for an undertaking with a market share below 35 percent: establish that it faces no significant competition, rebut its contrary arguments, and recognise its position as dominant.

This is the lead-in clause of a rule: it sets the case in which the criteria that follow apply (establishing the monopoly (dominant) position of several undertakings, except the cases in point 10.1.4), so it is the condition part of a criterion the AMCU applies, not a bare heading; it would be housekeeping only if read as a heading-like fragment that asserts nothing on its own.

It states the criteria the AMCU must establish for collective dominance (no or insignificant competition among the undertakings, and no significant competition or no competitors for them together), which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a step the AMCU must take in establishing collective dominance, namely rebutting (where present) the undertakings' arguments that there is significant competition between them and from competitors, which a decision applies to the facts of a case.
It is a bare heading-like item naming a sub-stage (recognising the dominant position of each of several undertakings) and asserts no criterion, so it only structures the text.

This is the lead-in to the restated Article 12 criteria: it says when the AMCU recognizes a monopoly (dominant) position, which is a threshold the analysis applies to the facts, so it is a norm rather than a bare definition or heading.

It sets out the 35 percent market-share threshold together with the rebuttal conditions (having competitors, being subject to significant competition), a presumption the analysis applies to establish dominance, even though it restates Article 12 of the statute.

It states collective-dominance thresholds (over 50% for the two or three largest undertakings, over 70% for the four or five largest) as a presumption the undertakings can rebut by proving significant competition, which the analysis applies to the facts of a case.

It states a criterion the AMCU applies to establish dominance below the 35 percent share threshold. Dominance is established when the undertaking fails to rebut the AMCU's arguments that it faces no significant competition, for instance because competitors hold small shares.

It sets the condition for establishing a collective monopoly (dominant) position: two or more undertakings fail to rebut the AMCU's arguments on lack of competition between them and from others. A decision can apply this presumption and burden-of-proof criterion to a case.

Although it opens by defining when an undertaking does not face significant competition, it goes on to list indicators of market power and circumstances in which absence of significant competition is presumed ('Вважається, що... зокрема, коли'), which are criteria a decision applies to establish dominance.
It lists additional indicators of market power that the AMCU considers when establishing a dominant position, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It authorizes a step the AMCU may take in the analysis (refining the product, geographic or temporal boundaries of the market) when proving or rebutting a monopoly (dominant) position, which a decision can apply to a case.

It lists the information sources the AMCU may use to establish a monopoly (dominant) position, and the protocol's hard-case rule types such a list as a norm, even though it also explains what each source means.
The proposition sets out the Methodology's subject matter, namely what it covers: the procedure by which AMCU bodies define a product market and establish a monopoly (dominant) position.

The proposition lists the proceedings and purposes in which the market is defined under the Methodology (concerted actions, concentrations, abuse of dominance, anticompetitive actions of authorities, market studies, other cases provided by law), which is the scope of application.

The proposition lists the proceedings and purposes (abuse cases, applications on concerted actions, concentrations, market studies, state control measures) in which dominance is determined under the Methodology, which is a statement of its field of application.
It is only a lead-in announcing that the terms which follow carry the stated meanings; it structures the text and does not itself define any term or say how the analysis is done.

It states what the term 'multi-sided market' (багатосторонній ринок) means, a product market where an undertaking mediates interaction between distinct customer groups whose demands affect each other, without saying how the analysis is done.

It states what the term 'barriers to exit' (бар’єри виходу з ринку) means by classifying the circumstances and administrative factors it covers, without stating how the market analysis is done or concluded.
It states what 'barriers to entry' means (circumstances preventing new undertakings from starting to compete with incumbents) without saying how the market analysis is done or concluded.
It states what the term 'interchangeability of goods' means without saying how the market analysis is carried out.

It states what the term 'upstream market' (висхідний ринок) means, classifying it as a market for goods necessary to produce or sell goods on another relevant market, without saying how the analysis is done.

It states what the term 'відповідний ринок' means (a product market, including an affected market, within defined product, geographic and temporal boundaries) without saying how the analysis is carried out.
It defines the term 'countervailing market power of a customer (supplier)', including the means by which such power can arise, without stating how the AMCU applies it in the analysis.
It states what the term 'discrimination of customers by suppliers' means without saying how a market is defined or dominance is established.
It says what 'differentiated goods' means, including when goods count as differentiated by territory, without saying how the AMCU defines a market or establishes dominance.

It states what the term 'допоміжний товар' (auxiliary product) means — a complement consumed with and acquired in connection with a main product — without stating how a market is defined or dominance established.
It states what the term 'загальнодержавний ринок' means (a product market whose geographic boundaries cover the territory of the state) without saying how the analysis is done, so it only classifies.

It says what the term 'задіяний ринок товару' (affected product market) means, namely the market where a concentration or competition-law infringement takes place or has effect; it only classifies and does not itself say how the market's boundaries are set.
The proposition defines the term 'замінність товарів' as one-directional substitutability and does not say how a market is defined or dominance is established.

It states what the term "замовник" (customer) means, a legal or natural person, including a buyer, that acquires and uses goods, services or works on the relevant product market, and it says nothing about how a market is defined or dominance is established.

It defines the term 'chain of substitution' (ланцюг замінності) and its minimum composition, classifying a type of substitutability without stating how the AMCU defines the market or treats such chains in the analysis.
It states what the term 'мережевий ефект' (network effect) means, distinguishing direct and indirect effects, without saying how the market analysis is carried out.

Although framed as a definition of a monopoly (dominant) position, it sets criteria the AMCU can apply to a case: no or no significant competition, barriers to entry, and collective-dominance share thresholds (three largest above 50 percent, five largest above 70 percent). Under the hard-case rules this makes it a norm.
It states what the term 'downstream market' (низхідний ринок) means without saying how a market is defined or dominance is established.

It states what the term 'основний товар' (main product) means, as a product consumed together with an auxiliary product that directly satisfies consumer needs, without saying how the market analysis is done.

It states what the term 'попит' (demand) means — customers' ability and willingness to buy a quantity of a product at a price within a territory and period — without saying how the market analysis is done.
It states what the term 'постачальник' (supplier) means, an undertaking offering goods for sale on the relevant product market, without saying how the market is defined or dominance established.
It states what the term 'пропозиція' (supply) means without saying how the market analysis is carried out.
It states what the term 'regional product market' means by classifying markets according to their geographic extent, without saying how a market is defined or dominance is established.

It states what the term 'ринкова влада' (market power) means, describing it as economic strength enabling independent conduct and price elevation, without itself prescribing how the AMCU conducts or concludes the analysis.

It states what 'market share' means (an undertaking's sales or purchases as a percentage of the total volume of the relevant market) without saying how the market is defined or how dominance is established.
It states what the term 'споживач' (consumer) means — a customer using the product without resale — without saying how a market is defined or dominance established.
It states what the term 'market structure' means (number of participants, their market shares, entry and exit barriers) without stating how the analysis is done or concluded.
It states what the term 'суб’єкти товарного ринку' (market participants) means by listing who they are, without saying how a market is defined or dominance is established.
It states what the term 'суміжний товарний ринок' means (an upstream and/or downstream market relative to the target product's market) without saying how the analysis is done.

It states what the term 'territorial (geographic) boundaries of the market' means (a territory with demand and supply for the target product, largely homogeneous conditions of competition, distinguishable from adjacent territories) without setting out a step, method or consequence of the analysis.

It says what the term 'товар' means, including zero-price products with economic value on multi-sided markets, and classifies what counts as a product without stating how a market is defined or dominance is established.

It defines the term 'товарні межі ринку' as a group of similar, homogeneous goods within which a customer can ordinarily switch between products, and it does not itself prescribe a step, method, or criterion for the analysis.
It states what the term 'трансакційні витрати' (transaction costs) means and says nothing about how a market is defined or dominance is established.
It states what the term 'умови конкуренції' (conditions of competition) means by listing its components and influencing factors, without saying how the market analysis is carried out.
It states what the term 'actual competitor' (фактичний конкурент) means without saying how the market is defined or dominance established.
It states what the term 'digital platform' means (an intermediary ICT system enabling two or more user groups to interact) without saying how a market is defined or dominance established.
It states what the term 'цільовий товар' (target product) means — the product under study or investigation — without saying how the market is defined or dominance established.
It states what the term 'temporal boundaries of the market' means without saying how the analysis is carried out.

It is a bare reference stating that listed terms carry the meanings given in the Law on the Protection of Economic Competition, which the protocol classes as a reference to the statute's own definitions rather than a definition stated in the text.

It lists, in order, the stages the AMCU must carry out to define the relevant product market (target product, suppliers and customers, product, geographic and temporal boundaries), which is a list of stages that tells the AMCU what to do and in what order.

It lists the stages the AMCU must carry out to establish a monopoly (dominant) position, in addition to the steps in point 1, which is a list of analysis stages telling the AMCU what to do and so counts as a norm under the hard-case rule.

It tells the AMCU how to carry out the analysis: the number and order of stages are set case by case, certain stages (subparagraphs 1 and 3–5 of point 1, and 1 and 8 of point 2) are mandatory, and certain steps are not applied for registered natural monopolies. These are procedural requirements a decision applies to a case, not a statement about which proceedings the Methodology covers.

It states a methodological rule the AMCU applies in a case: where a restriction of competition is established within the broader possible market, defining the market in narrower bounds is not required.

It lists what the analysis covers: undertakings, groups of undertakings, target products, product groups, market relations and public authorities insofar as they engage in economic activity. It sets no criterion or step for defining the market or establishing dominance.

It states how the AMCU determines the composition of the undertaking under analysis, by listing the entities linked by relations of control within the meaning of Article 1 of the Law, which is a method a decision applies to the facts.
It sets out the method the AMCU uses to determine the composition of a group of undertakings: listing the independent undertakings to which the entity dealing in the target product belongs.

It states the criterion by which the AMCU forms the list of products for market definition — products circulating in Ukraine or the relevant part of it that suppliers (customers) regard as substitutable or interchangeable — which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states the criteria (similarity of consumer characteristics, conditions of consumption, conditions of sale, and prices) by which the AMCU determines what constitutes a single product or product group, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

The proposition says what the term 'товар' (product) does not include, namely intermediate results that are consumed in the undertaking's own production rather than sold on the market, and it gives no method for defining a market or establishing dominance.

It states how the AMCU forms the list of main suppliers and customers, setting a 5% threshold for significant volumes with exceptions for 20+ or fewer than 6 similarly sized undertakings and a fallback rule for computing total volume, all of which a decision applies to the facts of a case.

It states the method by which the product boundaries of a market are defined, namely by assessing demand-side and, where necessary, supply-side substitutability, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states how the demand-side substitutability assessment is carried out (identify goods customers perceive as substitutes for the target product and assess their ability and willingness to switch when supply conditions change), which is a method a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It prescribes a step the AMCU takes when assessing supply-side substitutability—identifying undertakings able to start producing or selling the target or demand-substitutable product within at most two years—which is a criterion with a time threshold applicable to the facts of a case.
It lists the criteria by which demand-side substitutability of products is determined and the further evidence the AMCU analyses when needed, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a method the AMCU follows when assessing demand-side substitutability: identifying which criteria from point 4 are decisive for consumers switching between products, and forming the group of interchangeable goods from those criteria taken together.
It states a rule the AMCU applies to the facts of a case: where the target product has no substitute, the product boundaries of the market are set by the target product alone.

It states a general rule for delineating the product market — different stages of the distribution chain are, as a rule, not combined in one group of interchangeable products — which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a criterion the AMCU may apply in defining the product boundaries of a market, namely that the boundaries may be extended to include complementary products that are used together with the main product, necessary for its functioning, or significantly increase the efficiency of its use.

Beyond naming system, multiple and dual markets, it tells the AMCU how to set the product boundaries when there are auxiliary products: one combined market, separate markets for compatible subsets, or one separate market for all auxiliary products, which a decision can apply to a case.

It states a criterion for including non-substitute goods in the same product market (chains of substitution where price movements propagate and one good is the target product), which can be applied to the facts of a case.
It states a criterion for setting product boundaries: a set of differentiated products that are interchangeable for a particular group of customers forms a market within single product boundaries.
It states when a discriminated or non-discriminated group of buyers forms a separate, narrower product market, and sets cumulative conditions the AMCU can apply to the facts of a case.

It states criteria for defining the product boundaries of a market: highly novel goods may form a separate product market, and intensive R&D is taken into account when assessing homogeneity of competitive conditions, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It lists the circumstances, such as contractual obligations, switching costs, network effects and data-portability costs, that the AMCU can check against the facts of a case as obstacles to demand-side substitutability when defining the product boundaries of the market, so it gives applicable indicators and not just the meaning of a term.

It defines when supply-side substitutability arises (a price change prompts other undertakings to start producing a substitute within a short period, as a rule up to two years, without additional costs or risks), but it does not say what the AMCU does with such substitutability in defining the market.

It sets out cumulative conditions, including a two-year threshold for starting production or sales without investment, under which supply-side substitutability is found, which is a criterion a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a criterion for when supply-side substitutability is taken into account in defining market boundaries (if it creates competition for actual market participants, even if only some suppliers can or would switch), which a decision can apply to a case.

It states how product boundaries are determined in a case, allowing them to be defined differently for the same target product depending on which supplier's product is chosen, notably where one undertaking can unilaterally set conditions of circulation that constrain another, which is a methodological criterion a decision can apply to the facts.

It states what the term 'territorial (geographic) boundaries of the market' means (a territory with homogeneous conditions of competition, distinguishable from other territories) without prescribing any step, method or consequence for how the AMCU conducts the analysis.

It tells the AMCU bodies which indicators (product characteristics, suppliers, prices, entry barriers, transport costs, trade flows, etc.) they must assess when defining the geographic boundaries of a market, which is a criterion a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a criterion the AMCU takes into account when defining the geographic boundaries of a market (past actual switching of customers/suppliers to other territories), which can be applied to the facts of a case.

It tells the AMCU how to apply the indicators of homogeneous competitive conditions when defining the geographic market: together or separately, and case by case. The parenthetical list of proceedings only illustrates the occasions and does not set the Methodology's scope.

It states a method for defining the geographic market when suppliers have no stable ties to customers or cannot discriminate by location: the market is set from supplier locations by establishing on which neighbouring territories other suppliers of the target product or its substitutes are present.

It states a criterion the AMCU applies: when suppliers have stable ties with particular customers or can discriminate among them by location, the geographic market is defined according to where the customer is located.

It states how imports are treated in the analysis: import-source territories are not automatically included in the geographic market, importers are counted among suppliers, and their actual sales enter the calculation of market volume and shares, while potential imports are disregarded.

It sets a condition a decision can apply to a case: geographic market boundaries already defined by the AMCU may be revised when competition conditions change substantially, for example when conditions in separate areas converge and those areas merge into one geographic market.
It states a method the AMCU may apply (the SSNIP / hypothetical monopolist test) and the conditions under which that test is not applied, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states what the term 'temporal boundaries of the market' means: the period during which the relevant transactions form a product market with homogeneous conditions of competition. It does not say how the AMCU is to establish that period.

It sets a default one-year duration for the temporal boundaries of the market and states the conditions (differences in production/supply/purchase conditions, including regulatory ones, and periodic or seasonal fluctuations of demand and supply) under which the AMCU body may lengthen or shorten that period, which is a criterion a decision can apply to a case.

It sets out the method for calculating market volume (a summation formula over undertakings' volumes) and criteria for choosing value or physical indicators, including a 5 per cent price-divergence threshold and a rule for resolving conflicting results, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states the calculation method (a summation formula over the products within the market's product and temporal boundaries) for determining an undertaking's sales or purchase volume, which the AMCU applies to compute market volume and shares.
It sets out the formula by which the AMCU calculates the volume of a product sold or purchased by each undertaking, a method directly applicable to the facts of a case.
It sets out the formula by which an undertaking's market share is calculated (its sales or purchases divided by the market volume), a method the AMCU applies to the facts of a case.
It sets out the method (a formula with defined variables) by which the combined market share of the two to five largest undertakings is calculated, which a decision applies to the facts of a case.

It states how market share is calculated (percentage ratio of an undertaking's individual indicator to the market total) and lists which indicators to use depending on market characteristics, a method a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It sets a method for the analysis: undertakings' market shares are calculated over the period matching the temporal boundaries of the relevant product market, a rule a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states how market concentration is assessed, gives the method of calculating the CRs and HHI indices, and sets HHI thresholds and how to read their trend over time, which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It says which undertakings count as potential competitors, with the conditions (including the one-year entry horizon) that make up the term's meaning, but it does not say how the AMCU uses them in defining the market or establishing dominance.

It states how the AMCU establishes the effect of potential competition (analysis of entry/exit barriers and the likelihood, timeliness and effectiveness of entry), gives an indicator with a threshold (no new entry for two years or more, or beyond the investment cycle, may signal entry barriers), and prescribes how the possibility of entry is assessed, all of which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It says what counts as barriers to entry by listing their kinds (demand-side limits, administrative, environmental, economic and organisational factors, undeveloped infrastructure, other entry costs) without saying how the AMCU uses them to define a market or establish dominance.

It states a criterion the AMCU applies to the facts: if at least one entry barrier cannot be overcome within the two years needed to enter the market, the undertaking is treated as not being a potential competitor.

It says what the 'economic incentive to enter the market' means for a potential competitor: expected revenues exceed entry costs, including the cost of overcoming barriers. It does not itself tell the AMCU how to carry out or conclude the analysis.

It directs the AMCU to take countervailing buyer (supplier) power into account, lists the indicators of negotiating strength, and sets the condition (proof that it substantially limits or removes the undertaking's ability to set terms independently) under which it affects the finding of dominance.

It lists, in order, the steps the AMCU must take to establish a monopoly (dominant) position, and the steps include the Article 12 share thresholds (35/50/70 percent) that the analysis applies, so per the hard-case rules it is a norm.

It sets out the thresholds and rebuttable presumptions (35%, 50%, 70%, the one-year duration, the reversed burden of proof) that the AMCU applies to the facts of a case to establish a monopoly (dominant) position, and the statutory restatement does not change its type.

Beyond defining 'not subject to significant competition', it lists indicators of market power and states the circumstances in which the undertaking is deemed not to face significant competition, criteria a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It lists additional indicators the AMCU considers when establishing market power (concentration, entry barriers, share asymmetry, positions on adjacent markets, special rights, control of essential infrastructure), which a decision can apply to the facts of a case.

It states a step the AMCU may take in the analysis: while establishing or rebutting a dominant position, its bodies may refine the product, geographic or temporal boundaries of the market, which a decision can apply to a case.

It lists the information sources the AMCU uses to define the product market and establish dominance, and under the hard-case rules a list of information sources is a norm, even though it also explains what each source is.
